question: On 31 May, around 70 employees of the National Public Health Organisation were dismissed after subprojects 5 and 7 of the Spyros Doxiadis programme came to an end. The programme’s operation is up in the air, with tragic consequences for workers, as it is cofinanced by the EU’s Recovery and Resilience Fund. These are workers who served public health, covering permanent and ongoing needs.

The end of the programme is the direct result of the National Public Health Organisation operating on the basis of commercial criteria, bringing instability to the running of services that are critical for the people, the cause of this instability being the pursuit of ephemeral funds.

At the same time, these operating conditions exacerbate job insecurity for dozens of workers who are caught in a state of permanent temporariness, with fixed-term contracts reigning. In view of the above, can the Commission answer the following: 1.

Where does it stand on the fact that the pittance which the healthcare sector receives from EU funding is only occasional and temporary and does not make up for the need for high-quality free and public healthcare services for the people, including prevention, treatment and recovery?

Where does it stand on the need to hire permanent staff across all specialisms and to make all contract staff in healthcare facilities permanent, bearing in mind that the majority of workers in these services are caught in a state of permanent temporariness?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (27.8.2026) In accordance with Article 168(7) of the Treaty on the Functioning of the EU1, the responsibilities of the Member States include the management of health services and medical care and the allocation of the resources assigned to them.

The EU’s role is to support them in strengthening their health systems through funding, policy guidance, encouraging cooperation and exchange of best practices via technical assistance. Analysis, including under the European Semester, identified persistent shortages and uneven distribution of health professionals in Greece, hampering access to healthcare2.

Hence, the 2026 Council country-specific recommendation to Greece highlighted the need to tackle shortages of nurses and doctors3. The Recovery and Resilience Facility, as a temporary instrument (2020-2026), was established to help Member States address the economic and social impact of the COVID-19 crisis and its aftermath by promoting economic, social and territorial cohesion through reforms and investments4.

The Greek recovery and resilience plan includes several reforms and investments to strengthen its healthcare system, such as a reform of the primary health care system and the personal doctor reform5. Their long-term sustainability will be important to maximise lasting impact.

The Commission also supports Member States in addressing this challenge through EU4Health initiatives on health workforce planning6, retention of nurses7, improvement of mental health of health workers8. Without prejudging the outcome of the negotiations, the Commission’s proposal for the next multiannual financial framework also provides for funding opportunities on health.
